subject: Science
framework: National Curriculum in England (2014): Science programmes of study (Key Stages 1 to 3); Reception aligned to EYFS Understanding the World: The Natural World
statusNote: Key Stage 1, 2 and 3 statements were read from the gov.uk National Curriculum science programme of study; the whole page, including the end of the Key Stage 4 section, has now been read, and a sample of Year 2 to Year 6 statements was re-checked against the official primary PDF with no errors found. EYFS Understanding the World: The Natural World was read in the 13 July 2026 statutory framework (in force 1 September 2026) and the Reception row is consistent with it. Statutory content is set by key stage and by named year for KS1 and KS2; the Year 7 to Year 9 allocation and all unit titles are a recommended sequence because the National Curriculum sets Key Stage 3 content as a whole. Pages were read through a fetch tool that summarises text. Year 1 was rebuilt in November 2026 to the TGA Year 1 Curriculum Pack: one unit per half term, following Tarbiyyah Primary's Cornerstones projects (2026-27 order), White Rose maths and Little Wandle phonics.

purpose: Science builds understanding of the world through biology, chemistry and physics, with core knowledge, methods and uses.
Pupils develop key concepts that spark curiosity and help them explain, predict and analyse causes.
Pupils learn how scientific enquiry works so they can judge science's uses and implications now and later.
Precise technical vocabulary is expected, and schools may teach content earlier or later within a key stage.

statements: Explore the natural world, observe it and draw animals and plants.
Compare the natural world with contrasting environments.
Understand the seasons and changes in states of matter.
Ask simple questions that can be answered in different ways.
Observe closely using simple equipment and perform simple tests.
Identify and classify; use observations to suggest answers.
Gather and record data to help answer questions.
Name common wild and garden plants, including deciduous and evergreen trees; describe the basic structure of plants.
Name common fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals; classify carnivores, herbivores and omnivores.
Name and label human body parts and link them to the senses.
Distinguish living, dead and never-alive things; link habitats to the organisms in them.
Describe simple food chains and how organisms depend on each other.
Describe how seeds and bulbs grow; plants need water, light and suitable temperature.
Offspring grow into adults; animals need water, food and air; humans need exercise, diet and hygiene.
Distinguish an object from its material; name common materials and describe their simple properties.
Compare the suitability of materials for different uses.
Explore how solid objects change shape when squashed, bent, twisted or stretched.
Observe seasonal changes and describe weather and day length across the four seasons.
Ask relevant questions and use different types of enquiry, including simple fair tests.
Make careful observations and take accurate measurements in standard units.
Gather, record, classify and present data using keys, charts, tables and diagrams.
Report findings, draw simple conclusions, make predictions and suggest improvements.

strands.strand: Biology: plants, animals and living things
statements: Describe the functions of roots, stems, leaves and flowers; investigate how water moves through plants.
Explain the flower's role in pollination, seed formation and dispersal.
Animals need the right nutrition and cannot make their own food; skeletons and muscles support and move the body.
Group living things in different ways and use classification keys.
Recognise that changing environments can endanger living things.
Describe the human digestive system and teeth; build and interpret food chains with producers, predators and prey.

strands.strand: Chemistry: rocks and states of matter
statements: Compare and group rocks by appearance and properties; describe how fossils form; soil is rock and organic matter.
Group materials as solids, liquids and gases; observe changes of state when heated or cooled.
Describe evaporation and condensation in the water cycle and link evaporation rate to temperature.

strands.strand: Physics: light, forces, sound and electricity
statements: Light is needed to see; understand reflection, dangers of sunlight and how shadows form.
Compare how things move on different surfaces; distinguish contact forces from magnetic forces at a distance.
Describe magnets attracting and repelling, magnetic poles and magnetic materials.
Sounds come from vibrations travelling through a medium to the ear; link pitch and volume to the source.
Build series circuits, name their parts and predict whether a lamp will light.
Recognise that switches open and close circuits; identify conductors and insulators.
Plan different enquiries, identifying and controlling variables.
Measure with increasing accuracy and precision, repeating readings where appropriate.
Record complex data using tables and scatter, bar and line graphs.
Use results to predict outcomes, design further tests and report causal links and confidence.

strands.strand: Biology: life cycles, circulation and evolution
statements: Compare life cycles of a mammal, amphibian, insect and bird; describe plant and animal reproduction.
Describe the changes as humans develop to old age (TGA: puberty is taught from Year 7).
Classify living things into broad groups using observable features and give reasons.
Name parts of the circulatory system and describe the heart, blood vessels and blood.
Explain how diet, exercise, drugs and lifestyle affect the body.
Living things change over time; fossils reveal ancient life; adaptation can lead to evolution.
Offspring resemble but vary from their parents.

strands.strand: Chemistry: properties and changes of materials
statements: Compare and group materials by hardness, solubility, transparency, conductivity and magnetic response.
Explain dissolving and recover dissolved substances; choose separation methods such as filtering, sieving and evaporating.
Dissolving, mixing and changes of state are reversible.
Burning and reacting acid with bicarbonate make new materials and are usually not reversible.

strands.strand: Physics: Earth and space, forces, light and electricity
statements: Describe the movement of Earth and planets around the Sun and the Moon around Earth.
Use Earth's rotation to explain day and night and the Sun's apparent movement.
Gravity pulls unsupported objects towards Earth; describe air resistance, water resistance and friction.
Explain how levers, pulleys and gears let a small force have a greater effect.
Light appears to travel in straight lines; we see things by light they emit or reflect.
Shadows match the shape of the object casting them.
Link lamp brightness and buzzer volume to cells and voltage; use standard circuit symbols.
Value objectivity, accuracy, precision, repeatability and reproducibility; understand that theories change with new evidence and peer review.
Evaluate risks and plan tests with independent, dependent and control variables.
Use apparatus safely, record data, assess method reliability and apply sampling techniques.
Present data in tables and graphs, interpret patterns and evaluate random and systematic error.
Use SI units and IUPAC chemical nomenclature; use and derive equations; carry out simple statistics.

strands.strand: Biology: structure and function of living organisms
statements: Cells are the basic units of life; use a light microscope; compare plant and animal cells.
Organisation from cells to tissues, organs, systems and organisms; adaptations of single-celled organisms.
Diffusion moves materials in and between cells.
Skeletal and muscular systems: support, protection, movement and antagonistic muscles.
Healthy diet, energy requirements, dietary imbalance and deficiency disease; digestion and enzymes.
Gas exchange system, breathing model, effects of exercise, asthma and smoking; stomata in plants.
Human and plant reproduction; role of the placenta; effects of recreational drugs.

strands.strand: Biology: material cycles, interdependence, genetics and evolution
statements: Photosynthesis: reactants, products, leaf adaptations and importance for life and atmosphere.
Aerobic and anaerobic respiration release energy; compare reactants and products, including fermentation.
Organisms depend on each other in food webs; toxins can accumulate; insect pollination supports food security.
Heredity; chromosomes, genes and DNA, including contributions of Watson, Crick, Wilkins and Franklin.
Continuous and discontinuous variation; variation drives natural selection.
Environmental change can lead to extinction; biodiversity and gene banks matter.
Particle model explains solids, liquids, gases, gas pressure, changes of state and diffusion.
Atoms, elements and compounds; symbols and formulae; conservation of mass.
Pure and impure substances; separation by filtration, evaporation, distillation and chromatography.
Reactions rearrange atoms; word and symbol equations; combustion, thermal decomposition, oxidation and displacement.
Acids, alkalis, neutralisation, pH and indicators; acid and metal, acid and alkali reactions; catalysts.
Exothermic and endothermic changes (qualitative); periodic table, groups, periods and Mendeleev.
Reactivity series and extraction with carbon; properties of ceramics, polymers and composites.
Structure of the Earth, rock cycle, limited resources and recycling; atmosphere composition and carbon dioxide impact on climate.
Energy: compare food, fuel, appliance and household energy values; units J, kJ, W, kW and kWh.
Energy transfers by conduction, radiation and other processes; energy is conserved; simple machines trade force and distance.
Speed equals distance divided by time; distance-time graphs; relative motion.
Forces as interactions; balanced and unbalanced forces; moments; friction; air and water resistance; Hooke's law as a special case.
Non-contact forces: gravity, magnetism and static electricity.
Pressure in fluids: pressure equals force divided by area; atmospheric and liquid pressure; upthrust, floating and sinking.

strands.strand: Physics: waves, electricity, matter and space
statements: Waves: water waves are transverse; sound is a longitudinal vibration needing a medium; hearing ranges.
Light: ray model, reflection, refraction, lenses, the eye, colour and white light (qualitative).
Current electricity: current, potential difference, resistance, series and parallel circuits; resistance equals p.d. divided by current.
Static electricity and electric fields; magnetic fields, Earth's magnetism, electromagnets and motors (principles).
Matter: density, conservation of mass, Brownian motion, diffusion and internal energy.
Space physics: weight equals mass times gravitational field strength; seasons from Earth's tilt; stars, galaxies and light years.

toKS4: KS3 sets up the Pearson Edexcel GCSE (9-1) sciences: cells, organs and digestion lead to Biology Topics 1 and 2; variation, DNA and natural selection lead to Biology Topics 3 and 4; photosynthesis, respiration, ecosystems and plants lead to Biology Topics 6, 8 and 9. Particle model, separation, atoms, reactions and the periodic table feed Chemistry Topics 1 to 4 and 6; combustion, atmosphere and climate feed Chemistry Topic 8. Forces and motion, energy, waves, electricity, magnetism and space feed Physics Topics 2 to 5, 7 to 10 and 12 to 15. Working scientifically feeds all core practicals and AO3.

links.topic: Weather, seasons and the water cycle

Science supplies food chains and variation; Geography studies places and human impact.

links.topic: Rocks, the Earth's structure and the atmosphere
links.how: Rocks and soils early on, then rock cycle, Earth structure and climate.
Maths provides measurement, graphing and averages; Science uses them to analyse enquiry data.

links.topic: Ideas that changed science (Solar System models, DNA discovery)
links.how: History gives context to changing explanations; Science explains the models and evidence.
Science gives properties of materials and circuit rules; D&T applies them in making.
Computing supports sensors and spreadsheets used to collect and present science data.
English supports precise explanation and written reports.
Science explains light and colour; Art uses observation and drawing skills.
